title: Selective Funding Slows Startup Creation in India as VCs Shift From Volume to Quality
excerpt: New company formation drops 15–20% as venture capital concentrates on AI, deep tech, and climate, while consumer internet and edtech struggle to raise even pre-seed rounds.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's startup formation dropped 15-20% as VCs shift focus from volume to quality.
  • AI, deep tech, and climate tech are attracting most early-stage venture capital.
  • Global venture funding is 60% below 2021 peaks, reflecting a broader slowdown.
  • Founders are adapting by bootstrapping longer and seeking non-dilutive funding options.

  • India's startup ecosystem saw a 15–20% decline in new company formation over the past year as venture capital shifted from volume to selectivity
  • VCs are concentrating larger cheques into fewer companies, with AI, deep tech, and climate tech attracting the bulk of early-stage capital
  • The slowdown mirrors a global trend: total global venture funding remains 60% below 2021 peaks despite a recovery in late-stage mega-rounds
  • Indian founders are adapting by bootstrapping longer, targeting profitability earlier, and exploring non-dilutive funding through government grants and revenue-based financing

Fewer Startups, Bigger Bets

India's startup creation rate has slipped measurably over the past year as venture capital investors shift from the spray-and-pray approach of the 2021 boom to a far more selective strategy, according to The Economic Times. New company registrations with startup-oriented structures are down an estimated 15–20% year-on-year, with the sharpest declines in consumer internet, edtech, and e-commerce — sectors that attracted outsized funding during the pandemic-era surge.

The data does not suggest Indian VCs are leaving the market. Instead, they are concentrating larger cheques into fewer companies. Early-stage rounds are taking longer to close, term sheets carry more founder-unfriendly provisions, and the bar for traction before raising a seed or Series A has risen substantially. The median time from incorporation to first institutional raise has stretched from eight months to over 14 months.

Where the Money Is Going

AI and generative AI startups continue to command disproportionate attention from both domestic and global investors. Deep tech ventures in semiconductors, space, and defense — areas where India's government has introduced dedicated incentive programs — are also seeing sustained interest. Climate tech and sustainability, buoyed by India's 2070 net-zero commitment and the green hydrogen push, round out the sectors where capital flows remain healthy.

"The ecosystem is maturing. Investors are no longer funding ideas — they're funding businesses with real revenue, real unit economics, and a clear path to profitability."

— Venture Capital Industry Observer

The corollary is that sectors without clear AI or deep-tech tailwinds are struggling. Consumer social apps, horizontal SaaS platforms without differentiation, and quick-commerce clones are finding it increasingly difficult to raise even pre-seed capital. The "unicorn factory" narrative that defined Indian tech from 2019 to 2022 has been replaced by a more measured emphasis on durable business models.

The Oxford Warning

A recent Oxford Economics study flagged that restrictive digital regulations could compound the funding slowdown, estimating that heavy-handed policy frameworks could cut Indian startup formation by an additional 20%. The research highlighted how data localization requirements, compliance costs, and regulatory uncertainty add friction that disproportionately burdens early-stage companies with limited resources.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian-origin entrepreneurs in the U.S. and elsewhere who may be considering a return to build in India, the environment has changed. The easy-money era is over, but the infrastructure for building serious technology companies — talent availability, digital public infrastructure, government procurement programs, and a 1.4-billion-person domestic market — remains among the strongest in any emerging economy.

NRI investors with exposure to Indian venture funds should expect slower portfolio construction and longer hold periods, but potentially stronger returns per investment as the quality bar rises. The era of 30 startups per fund has given way to concentrated portfolios of 12–15 carefully selected companies — a structure more familiar to Silicon Valley investors than to those who entered Indian VC during the boom years.
